title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
directAnswer: Don't merge — binary search a *partition*. Split the combined arrays into a left part and a right part of the right sizes so that everything on the left ≤ everything on the right. Binary search the cut position in the smaller array (the cut in the larger one is then forced), checking the four border elements. When `leftA ≤ rightB` and `leftB ≤ rightA`, the median falls out of those four values. O(log(min(m, n))) time, O(1) space.

remember.pattern: Binary search the partition of the smaller array
remember.formula:
ensure A is the shorter array
half = (m + n + 1) // 2
lo, hi = 0, m
while lo <= hi:
    i = (lo + hi) // 2          # cut in A
    j = half - i               # cut in B
    Aleft  = A[i-1] if i>0 else -inf;  Aright = A[i] if i<m else +inf
    Bleft  = B[j-1] if j>0 else -inf;  Bright = B[j] if j<n else +inf
    if Aleft <= Bright and Bleft <= Aright: # correct cut
        if (m+n) odd: return max(Aleft, Bleft)
        return (max(Aleft,Bleft) + min(Aright,Bright)) / 2
    elif Aleft > Bright: hi = i - 1
    else: lo = i + 1
rules: Always binary search the **smaller** array so the range is `[0, min(m, n)]` → `O(log(min(m, n)))`.
The cut in B is **derived**: `j = (m + n + 1) // 2 − i`, so the left side always holds exactly half the elements.
Guard the borders with `±∞` when a cut sits at index 0 or the array end — this removes every empty-side special case.
Correct partition condition is `Aleft ≤ Bright AND Bleft ≤ Aright`; if `Aleft > Bright` move the A-cut left, else move it right.
Use `(m + n + 1) // 2` so the **left** side has the extra element on odd total — then the odd-median is `max(Aleft, Bleft)` with no extra arithmetic.
whenToUse: Median / k-th element across two (or more) sorted arrays in sub-linear time
Strict `O(log(m+n))` requirement that rules out merging
Any 'find the split that balances two sorted sequences' framing
antiSignals: O(m + n) is acceptable → just merge with two pointers; far less error-prone
Arrays are unsorted → sort or use selection; binary-search partition needs sorted input

remember.takeaway: The leap is to stop thinking 'merge then index' and start thinking 'where do I cut?'. Binary searching a partition — with ±∞ sentinels erasing the edge cases — is the canonical O(log) technique for order-statistics across sorted inputs.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can reach the O(log(min(m,n))) partition method (or at least the O(log(m+n)) k-th element method) and handle the brutal edge cases — empty sides, odd/even totals, equal borders — without bugs.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Binary searching the larger array (wrong complexity), mishandling the empty-partition borders (index out of bounds), or botching the odd/even median formula.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the merge baseline and its O(m+n), then pivot to 'binary search the cut', explain the ±∞ sentinel trick that kills all the edge cases, and derive j from i so the left half size is fixed.

problemStatement:
Given two sorted arrays `nums1` and `nums2` of size `m` and `n` respectively, return **the median** of the two sorted arrays.

The overall run time complexity should be `O(log (m+n))`.
understanding: The median splits all m+n values into a lower half and an upper half of equal size. We never build the merged array; instead we find a 'cut' through both arrays so the lower half has the right count and every lower element ≤ every upper element. The four elements straddling the cut give the median.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can one of the arrays be empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — m or n can be 0 (but not both). The ±∞ sentinels at the borders make an empty array behave correctly with no special-casing.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the total length odd or even — how does that change the answer?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Odd total → median is the single middle element (max of the two left borders). Even total → average of the two middle elements (max of left borders and min of right borders).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do the arrays share values or have duplicates?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Both possible. The partition condition uses ≤, so equal border values still satisfy a valid cut.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is O(m+n) acceptable, or must it be logarithmic?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The prompt insists on O(log(m+n)). I'll present the merge baseline for clarity, then deliver the O(log(min(m,n))) partition solution that meets the bound.

approaches.name: Binary Search the Partition (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Frame it as 'binary search the cut in the smaller array' and emphasize the ±∞ sentinels.
hints: Imagine drawing one vertical cut through each array so that the combined left side has exactly half the elements. What must be true about the four values touching the cut for it to be the median split?
Fix the total left-size to (m+n+1)/2. Then the cut position j in B is forced once you choose the cut i in A — so you only search i.
Search i in the SMALLER array. A cut is valid when Aleft ≤ Bright and Bleft ≤ Aright. If Aleft > Bright, your A-cut is too far right; otherwise too far left. Use ±∞ for out-of-range borders.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Binary search over the cut position in the smaller array (length min(m, n)) → log₂(min(m, n)) iterations, O(1) work each. No extra memory beyond a few variables.
approaches.explanation:
Find, without merging, a partition that places exactly the lower half of all elements on the left.

**Reframe the median as a cut.** A median splits the `m + n` values into a left part and a right part where (a) the left part has a fixed size and (b) every left value ≤ every right value. If we cut `nums1` after index `i` (so `i` elements of A go left) and `nums2` after index `j` (so `j` elements of B go left), then the left part has `i + j` elements. We *want* the left part to hold `half = (m + n + 1) / 2` elements (the `+1` puts the extra element on the left for odd totals), so once we pick `i`, the cut `j = half - i` is **forced**. That reduces a two-dimensional search to a one-dimensional binary search over `i`.

**Search the smaller array.** We binary search `i` in `[0, m]` after swapping so that A is the shorter array. This bounds the work at `O(log(min(m, n)))` and keeps `j = half - i` within `[0, n]` (guaranteed when `m <= n`).

**The four border values.** Around the cut sit `Aleft = A[i-1]`, `Aright = A[i]`, `Bleft = B[j-1]`, `Bright = B[j]`. When a cut lands at the very start (`i == 0`) there is no left element, so we treat `Aleft = -∞`; at the end (`i == m`) there is no right element, so `Aright = +∞`; likewise for B. These **sentinels are the trick that erases every empty-partition edge case** — no special branches for empty arrays or cuts at the boundary.

**The validity condition.** Because each array is individually sorted, `Aleft <= Aright` and `Bleft <= Bright` automatically. The cut is the correct global split exactly when the *cross* conditions also hold: `Aleft <= Bright` and `Bleft <= Aright`. That means every element on the left (the max of which is `max(Aleft, Bleft)`) is ≤ every element on the right (the min of which is `min(Aright, Bright)`).

**Driving the search.** If `Aleft > Bright`, we took too many large elements from A into the left — move the A-cut left: `hi = i - 1`. If instead `Bleft > Aright` (the only other failure), the A-cut is too far left — move it right: `lo = i + 1`. Otherwise we've found the cut.

**Reading off the median.** With a valid cut: if `m + n` is **odd**, the left side has the extra element, so the median is `max(Aleft, Bleft)`. If **even**, it's the average of the two central values: `(max(Aleft, Bleft) + min(Aright, Bright)) / 2`. The `(m + n + 1) / 2` choice of `half` is what makes the odd case this clean.

**Why it terminates correctly.** The window `[lo, hi]` on `i` strictly shrinks each iteration, and a valid partition always exists, so the loop returns from inside on the correct cut.
approaches.insight: The reframing — from 'merge and index' to 'find the balancing cut' — is the transferable idea. Deriving one cut from the other collapses the search to one dimension, and the ±∞ sentinels turn a notoriously edge-case-heavy problem into a handful of clean comparisons. The same partition-search mindset solves the generalised 'k-th element of two sorted arrays' and median-of-streams variants.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Searching the longer array
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Binary searching the larger array makes complexity O(log(max(m,n))) and lets the derived cut j = half - i fall outside [0, n], causing wrong borders or crashes. Always swap so the searched array is the shorter one.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
m, n = len(nums1), len(nums2)
# no swap — searches nums1 even if it is the longer array
half = (m + n + 1) // 2
lo, hi = 0, m
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if len(nums1) > len(nums2):
    nums1, nums2 = nums2, nums1
m, n = len(nums1), len(nums2)
half = (m + n + 1) // 2
lo, hi = 0, m

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing boundary sentinels
commonMistakesDetailed.why: When a cut sits at index 0 or the array end, the missing border element must act as ±∞. Reading nums[i] or nums[i-1] directly throws an index error and breaks empty-array inputs.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
int aLeft = nums1[i - 1];   // crashes when i == 0
int aRight = nums1[i];      // crashes when i == m
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
int aLeft  = (i == 0) ? Integer.MIN_VALUE : nums1[i - 1];
int aRight = (i == m) ? Integer.MAX_VALUE : nums1[i];

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Integer division in the even case
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The median of an even-length total is generally a non-integer (e.g. 2.5). Dividing the sum of the two middle values by an integer 2 truncates the fraction.
